planTheory.hypothesis: This learner most likely holds multiplication as a procedure attached to a fact table rather than as a structure that can be read off a situation. The page is built to break that: item 6 offers an additive and a sharing distractor for the same numbers, item 5 hides a repeated group inside a two-step story, item 7 rewards deriving 45 from a neighbor fact instead of retrieving it, and items 4 and 8 demand that one total be seen as more than one rectangle. So the diagnostic question is not "can the learner multiply within 48" but "can the learner decide what kind of multiplicative question is being asked, and move flexibly between total, factors, and array." The theory is that performance will hold on forward equal-groups items and degrade on inverse and multi-representation items (ASM-04, ASM-05), with fact recall as a confounder that must be measured separately (ASM-02) so a structural error is never misread as a computation slip. Because the entire evidence base is empty — no math accuracy, no fact bank, no prior decisions, no support observations — the smallest coherent program must sample every face of the construct once (forward equal groups, inverse/missing factor, array-to-equations, factor-pair generation, structure discrimination, derived fact) at Grade 3 depth, so a single pass separates the recall hypothesis from the structure hypothesis. Confirmation looks like clean forward work with breakdown concentrated in inverse and factor-pair items; disconfirmation looks like uniform difficulty across all six faces, which would relocate the target to fact fluency and the prerequisite band, or uniform success, which would push the construct toward multi-digit and multi-step extensions above Grade 3.
planTheory.intervention: Creator is the newly hired Festival Engineer aboard Nova Station, a space outpost where alien families are arriving for the once-a-year Starlight Festival. The station's power grid runs on equal groups: lantern racks, snack pods, badge crates, and light walls only switch on when their groups are counted and wired correctly. Every solved problem sends visible power down the station's glowing conduits, lighting up another district of the festival. The chapter opens in the Arrival Dock (three shared activities that restore basic power), then Creator chooses one of two festival wings to bring fully online — the Light Wall Wing, where power is arranged in glowing grids, or the Market Wing, where power flows through the stories of the stall-keepers. A final optional Repair Bay lets Creator fix miswired circuits other engineers got wrong. When a wing is complete, the festival launches: the whole station lights up and alien crowds pour in under a drone-lantern sky.

plannerRationale.agencyDesign: Four baseline measurement nodes plus Mystery choice plus locked Quest/Boss destinations. A live counter shows lanterns used vs. budget (e.g., 21/24), and an equation strip auto-drafts beneath the build (e.g., '3 × 8 = ?') which the child must complete and sign. Uneven rows physically sag and spark, making 'equal rows using the whole total' a visible engineering constraint, not a rule to remember.
engagementDimensions: Whether a visual, build-a-grid entry (picture-first) holds this learner through the harder inverse and factor-pair items better than a narrative entry — testing the mixed-learning-style hypothesis with a concrete visual anchor.

nodes.label: Market Wing: The Stall-Keepers' Missing Numbers
nodes.mechanic: Each stall is one item: a keeper states a short problem aloud (text mirrored, tap-to-replay), and the child answers by dialing a number into an equation socket, typing a value, or — on the capstone — assembling the missing-factor equation themselves from socket parts before solving it and naming the verifying fact. Correct sockets close the stall's circuit: lights, music, and smell-wisps all switch on at once, and the keeper begins actually selling to the crowd.
engagementDimensions: Whether keeping every item inside one continuous market story (narrative-first) lowers switching cost and sustains attention across the inverse band better than the grid-building entry — testing whether text is a hook or a barrier for this learner.

nodes.label: Market Wing: The Double-Shift Night
nodes.mechanic: Each item is a supply order for a two-occasion story. The child computes totals on the order-pad, and on structure items builds the delivery plan on a two-panel planning board — MORNING and AFTERNOON panels — by placing equation tiles (4 × 5 = 20 in each panel, then ×2 to the night total, or the combined 4 × 10 = 40 across both). Deliveries then physically run: hover-crates drop the ordered amount at each booth across both shifts, so an under-order is visible as afternoon booths left empty-handed.

planTheory.hypothesis: This learner most likely holds multiplication as a procedure attached to a fact table rather than as a structure that can be read off a situation. The page is built to break that: item 6 offers an additive and a sharing distractor for the same numbers, item 5 hides a repeated group inside a two-step story, item 7 rewards deriving 45 from a neighbor fact instead of retrieving it, and items 4 and 8 demand that one total be seen as more than one rectangle. So the diagnostic question is not "can the learner multiply within 48" but "can the learner decide what kind of multiplicative question is being asked, and move flexibly between total, factors, and array." The theory is that performance will hold on forward equal-groups items and degrade on inverse and multi-representation items (ASM-04, ASM-05), with fact recall as a confounder that must be measured separately (ASM-02) so a structural error is never misread as a computation slip. Because the entire evidence base is empty — no math accuracy, no fact bank, no prior decisions, no support observations — the smallest coherent program must sample every face of the construct once (forward equal groups, inverse/missing factor, array-to-equations, factor-pair generation, structure discrimination, derived fact) at Grade 3 depth, so a single pass separates the recall hypothesis from the structure hypothesis. Confirmation looks like clean forward work with breakdown concentrated in inverse and factor-pair items; disconfirmation looks like uniform difficulty across all six faces, which would relocate the target to fact fluency and the prerequisite band, or uniform success, which would push the construct toward multi-digit and multi-step extensions above Grade 3.
planTheory.intervention: Creator is the newly hired Festival Engineer aboard Nova Station, a space outpost where alien families are arriving for the once-a-year Starlight Festival. The station's power grid runs on equal groups: lantern racks, snack pods, badge crates, and light walls only switch on when their groups are counted and wired correctly. Every solved problem sends visible power down the station's glowing conduits, lighting up another district of the festival. The chapter opens in the Arrival Dock (three shared activities that restore basic power), then Creator chooses one of two festival wings to bring fully online — the Light Wall Wing, where power is arranged in glowing grids, or the Market Wing, where power flows through the stories of the stall-keepers. A final optional Repair Bay lets Creator fix miswired circuits other engineers got wrong. When a wing is complete, the festival launches: the whole station lights up and alien crowds pour in under a drone-lantern sky.
falsifyCriteria: Real child evidence contradicts the theory.
